pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Objects vs Materials

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials'):** Pupils should be taught to "distinguish between an object and the material from which it is made." The non-statutory guidance frames Year 1 as a time to "explore, name, discuss and raise and answer questions about everyday materials so that they become familiar with the names of materials and properties such as: hard/soft; stretchy/stiff; shiny/dull; rough/smooth; bendy/not bendy; waterproof/not waterproof; absorbent/not absorbent; opaque/transparent."

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-1, partial anchor):** There is no NGSS performance expectation dedicated to the object/material distinction; it is a UK-led foundation. The nearest DCI is PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]," which underpins 2-PS1-1 ("[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]").

- **Operational details:** Teach through hands-on sorting of real classroom objects: name each object (chair, cup, spoon, window) and then ask the separate question "what is it MADE OF?" Make the two questions visibly distinct so children stop treating the object's name and its material as the same word. Use the canonical Oak National demonstration of three identical water bottles — one plastic, one glass, one metal — to show one object made from different materials, and a spoon that could be metal, wood or plastic to show the same. Extend to objects made from more than one material (a pencil = wood + graphite + metal + rubber). Keep talk grounded in touch-and-look evidence, not definitions.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). Given a real object, the child can name it AND separately name the material it is made from, and can give an example of one object (e.g. a cup) made from two different materials — showing the object and its material are held apart in thought.
bestPractices: Ask the two questions separately and explicitly — "What is this?" (object) then "What is it made of?" (material) — so children learn the words 'object' and 'material' name different things; the everyday sense of 'material' as only cloth/fabric is a known blocker to overcome.
Use plentiful real objects to handle and sort, not pictures alone; concrete exploration is the KS1 norm and lets children reason from touch and sight.
Show the same object in different materials side by side (three water bottles: plastic, glass, metal) so children abstract that the object stays the same while the material changes.
Present objects made from more than one material (a pencil, a shoe, a window frame) to break the 'one object = one material' rule.
Use comparison of two same-material examples of different shape/size (per Hardy et al. 2020) to help children attend to material kind rather than to size, weight or shape.
Elicit ideas first with questioning or Concept Cartoons before correcting, treating a misconception as 'a concept in embryo' rather than simply wrong.
keyRepresentations: Real everyday objects to handle: chair, cup, spoon, window, pencil, shoe
The 'same object, different material' trio — three identical water bottles in plastic, glass and metal
Sorting mats / frequency tables that pair each object with its material
A two-column 'object | material' talk frame that keeps the two ideas visibly separate
One-object-many-materials exemplars (a pencil labelled wood + graphite + metal + rubber)
commonMisconceptions: Children conflate the object with the material, treating 'rock' or 'chair' as if the name of the thing and the name of the stuff are one and the same (an explicit KS1 statutory hurdle).
'Material' means only fabric/cloth — so children think building materials, glass or water are not 'materials'.
An object can only be made from one material (a pencil is 'wood', ignoring the graphite, metal ferrule and rubber).
A given object is always made from the same material — e.g. 'all spoons are metal', 'all cups are the same'.
When reasoning about objects, children fixate on salient surface features (size, weight, shape) rather than material kind, even though they can usually name the material (Hardy et al. 2020).

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds, teach the object/material distinction (UK KS1 Y1 'Everyday materials') through hands-on naming and sorting of real objects: name the thing, then separately ask 'what is it MADE OF?'. The core insight is that the same kind of object can be made from different materials (three bottles of the same kind, one plastic, one glass, one metal), and that one object can be made from several materials (a typical pencil with an eraser = wood + graphite core + metal + rubber). Keep talk grounded in touch-and-look evidence, not definitions, and overcome the everyday blocker that 'material' means only cloth.

activities.title: Two questions: 'What is it?' then 'What is it made of?'
feedback: If a child answers 'What is this?' with a material ('it's the metal one' / 'it's wood'), hold up two different objects made of the same material (a wooden spoon and a wooden block): 'same stuff, different things' — then name object and material separately for each.

If a child says the metal spoon 'isn't made of a material' or that 'material' means cloth, broaden the word explicitly: 'material means whatever something is made of — wood, metal, glass, plastic and cloth are all materials', then re-sort the tray naming each material.
Praise answers that keep the two words apart: 'Yes — the OBJECT is a spoon, and the MATERIAL is metal.'
activities.rationale: KS1 statutory requirement is to distinguish an object from the material it is made from, and the non-statutory guidance frames Year 1 as a time to explore, name and discuss real everyday materials. Asking the two questions separately targets the known blocker that children treat the thing's name and its stuff as one word, and that 'material' is taken to mean only fabric.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Y1 statutory requirement: pupils taught to 'distinguish between an object and the material from which it is made'; non-statutory property vocabulary list (hard/soft, shiny/dull, etc.).
Documented KS1 misconceptions: children confuse object with material; 'material' taken to mean only fabric; objects thought to be one material only or always the same material.
learnerActions: Handle real classroom objects (cup, spoon, pencil, shoe on a tray; touch and look at a chair and a window frame where they are).
For each object, first answer out loud 'What is this?' (name the object), then answer the separate question 'What is it made of?' (name the material).
Use a two-column 'object | material' talk frame or sorting mat so the two answers are placed in visibly different spots.

Sort the objects into material bins (wood, plastic, metal, glass, fabric, rubber/other), saying the object name and material name for each as you place it; an object made of more than one material (e.g. a pencil or a shoe) can go in more than one bin, or be talked through part by part.
activities.intendedInsight: The name of a thing and the name of the stuff it is made from are two different words answering two different questions; 'material' means whatever something is made of — wood, metal, glass, plastic and cloth are all materials.

activities.title: Same object, different material
feedback: If a child insists a spoon 'is always metal' or that an object can only be one material, let them handle real examples of the same object in several materials (plastic/glass/metal cup; wooden/plastic/metal spoon) and re-state object vs material for each.
When a child offers their own example of an object made from a different material, confirm the move: 'Right — it's still a cup, but the material has changed.'
activities.rationale: Side-by-side comparison of the same object in different materials helps children abstract that object identity holds while material varies, breaking the 'a given object is always made from the same material' misconception. This is the canonical Oak National three-bottle demonstration.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: children confuse object with material; 'material' taken to mean only fabric; objects thought to be one material only or always the same material.
learnerActions: Examine three bottles that look like the same object but are made of different materials — one plastic, one glass, one metal — handling and looking at each.
Answer the pair of questions: 'Are these the same object?' (yes, all bottles) and 'Are they the same material?' (no — plastic, glass, metal).
Do the same with a spoon that could be metal, wood or plastic.
Suggest a fresh example of one object that could be made from more than one material (e.g. a cup, a chair).
activities.intendedInsight: The same object can be made from different materials — the object stays the same while the stuff changes.

activities.title: One object, many materials
feedback: If a child names only the most obvious material (a pencil is 'wood'), prompt: 'Look again — what is the pointy bit made of? What is the pink end made of?' until all the materials are found.
Confirm the rule-break: 'A pencil isn't just wood — it's wood AND graphite AND metal AND rubber.'
activities.rationale: Presenting objects made from more than one material breaks the 'an object can only be made from one material' misconception, which the source lists as a documented KS1 hurdle.
sourceClaims: Documented KS1 misconceptions: children confuse object with material; 'material' taken to mean only fabric; objects thought to be one material only or always the same material.
learnerActions: Look closely at a pencil and find each separate part: the wooden body, the graphite core, the metal ferrule, the rubber eraser.
Name the material of each part, discovering this pencil is made from several materials (four here: wood, graphite, metal, rubber), not one.
Try the same with a shoe or a window frame, listing every material you can find in it.
If using a sorting activity, place a multi-material object (the pencil) into more than one material bin — 'this one needs more than one bin!'
activities.intendedInsight: One object can be made from more than one material, so you cannot assume 'one object = one material'.

activities.title: Attend to material, not size or shape
feedback: If a child groups objects by size or shape instead of material, draw attention back: 'These two are different sizes — but what are they both MADE of?'
Reinforce when the child names the shared material across different shapes/sizes.
activities.rationale: Hardy et al. (2020) found that comparing two same-material standards helps young children induce 'material kind' and reduces reliance on size, shape and weight; children can often name a material yet still reason from surface features. Note the study's context was a float/sink task with preschoolers, not this exact classroom activity.
sourceClaims: Comparing two same-material standards helps preschoolers induce 'material kind' for float/sink and reduces reliance on size/shape/weight; children can name materials yet still reason from surface features; adding labels gave no benefit beyond the two-object comparison.
learnerActions: Compare two objects made of the same material but different in shape or size (e.g. a wooden spoon and a wooden block, or a small and a large wooden item).
Say what is the SAME about them (the material) even though they look different.
Then compare two objects of the same shape but different material, and say what is DIFFERENT (the material).
activities.intendedInsight: What something is made of is a different question from how big, heavy or what shape it is; the material kind can stay the same even when size and shape change.

activities.title: Check-up: point, name, and transfer
feedback: Full grasp looks like: reliably naming object and material separately AND offering a fresh unprompted example that the same object can be built from different materials.
Partial grasp looks like: naming object and material for a single item when prompted, but not yet seeing that the SAME object can be made from different materials — treating each item in isolation.

Gap looks like: using one word for both ('it's wood'), giving a material when asked for the object, or insisting an object is always one fixed material. Reteach with the same-material/different-object pair, then same-object/different-material examples.
activities.rationale: The two-spoons stimulus keeps the kind of object the same while the material differs (real spoons may also differ in colour, size or shape), so it focuses attention on the object/material distinction; a child who conflated them answers 'which is the object?' with a material word or insists a spoon must be one material. These are assessment prompts from the source, used here during teaching as a self-check, not only as a scored test.
learnerActions: Point to any object in the room and say both the object name AND the material it is made from.
Given a wooden spoon and a metal spoon, point to the OBJECT, then say what MATERIAL each is made from, then answer 'Could I make this same spoon out of something else?'

Compare a teddy and a wooden train: say whether they are the same OBJECT (no — a teddy and a train) and whether they are the same MATERIAL (no — one is fabric, one is wood), keeping the two questions apart.

Answer a probing question such as: 'If I melted this plastic cup into a blob, is it still a cup? Is it still plastic?' (the object can stop existing while the material stays) — use this as a talking point, not a strict right/wrong test.
Discuss: 'Could a spoon be made of glass? Why might we not choose glass for a spoon?'
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who holds the distinction separates the thing (and its job) from the stuff it is made of, and can transfer the idea to fresh examples and to cases where the object changes but the material persists.

constraints: Keep all talk grounded in touch-and-look evidence from real objects, not definitions; concrete handling and sorting is the KS1 norm at this age.
Pre-readers need heavy audio/spoken scaffolding; avoid reading-dependent tasks.
Elicit children's ideas first (questioning or Concept Cartoons) before correcting, treating a misconception as 'a concept in embryo' rather than simply wrong.

A picture-only or tap-to-reveal screen scene is a useful scaffold for the two-question move and the same-object/different-material contrast — for example a material-swap/re-skin surface where a bottle stays the same bottle while its skin changes (turning see-through for glass or shiny for metal) — but it is not a substitute for handling and sorting real objects; recognition/matching responses do not by themselves elicit the independent naming and fresh-example production that signals full grasp.
A linear scored matching/sorting quiz can assess the distinction but does not by itself build it; use such formats as a check-up alongside hands-on exploration.

There is no NGSS performance expectation dedicated to the object/material distinction; it is a UK-led foundation. The nearest DCI is PS1.A ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-1]'), underpinning 2-PS1-1.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the cited sources were marked verified:false in the original row (NGSS 2-PS1-1 and the Oak National / STEM Learning misconceptions list); treat claims drawn from them as unconfirmed.

The Hardy et al. (2020) finding comes from a float/sink task with preschoolers and concerns inducing 'material kind'; it supports attending to material over surface features but does not directly establish efficacy for this specific KS1 object/material naming activity. Note also the source's point that adding labels gave no benefit beyond the two-object comparison.

Original row framed an interactive tap-to-reveal image as the primary 'teacher' and rated conversation and 3D as 'poor'; these are catalog-format preferences, not established pedagogical laws. This rewrite preserves the hands-on priority but does not assert that any single medium uniquely teaches or that 3D 'adds nothing'.

The 'melt the plastic cup into a blob' probe assumes the melted plastic remains the same material; for a thermoplastic this is roughly true, but it glosses over whether a child cleanly distinguishes 'is it still a cup?' from 'is it still plastic?' — use it conversationally, not as a strict right/wrong test.

The check-up activity's sourceClaims was set to [] because the original DfE claim supports the distinction as an objective but does not directly support the assessment-discrimination (two-spoons stimulus) rationale of that activity; no original claim directly backs that design point.

probeDeeper: If I melted this plastic cup down into a blob, is it still a cup? Is it still plastic? (object can stop existing while the material stays)
Point to anything in the room and tell me both the object AND the material it's made of.
Here's a teddy and a wooden train — are they the same OBJECT? Are they the same MATERIAL?
Could a spoon ever be made of glass? Why might we not choose glass for a spoon?
assess.correctAnswer: The OBJECT is the spoon (the thing, what it's for); the MATERIALS are wood and metal (the stuff each is made of). Yes — the same object (a spoon, a cup, a chair) can be made from different materials.

errorPatterns.pattern: Object and material are the same thing — the child answers 'what is the object?' with the stuff it's made of ('it's the metal one', 'it's wood') and has no separate word for the thing versus the stuff.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: hold up two DIFFERENT objects made of the SAME material (wooden spoon + wooden block) — 'same stuff, different things' — then two same objects of different material, naming object then material each time.
errorPatterns.distractor: This one isn't a spoon, it's just metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to point to the OBJECT, names a material instead; uses one word to cover both.

errorPatterns.pattern: An object can only ever be one material — 'a spoon is metal, that's what a spoon is'; denies you could make the same object from something else.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show real examples of one object in several materials (plastic/glass/metal cup; wooden/plastic/metal spoon); let the child handle them and re-state object vs material for each.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't make that spoon out of anything else — a spoon is always metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the idea that the same spoon/chair/cup could be made from a different material.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Material' means only cloth or fabric — the child reserves the word for soft textile-type stuff and won't call wood, metal or glass a 'material'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Broaden the word explicitly: 'material means whatever something is made of — wood, metal, glass, plastic and cloth are all materials'; sort a tray naming the material of each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked the material of the metal spoon, says it isn't made of a material / 'material' is what clothes are made of.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a single word for both the thing and the stuff ('it's wood'); when asked for the object, gives a material; insists an object is always one fixed material.
responseLevels.full: Reliably distinguishes the object (what it is / its job) from the material (what it's made of), AND transfers the idea: states the same object can be built from different materials and offers a fresh example unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Names the object and the material separately for a single item when prompted, but does not yet grasp that the SAME object can be made from different materials — treats each item in isolation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a wooden spoon and a metal spoon on the table. Say: 'Both of these are spoons. Point to the OBJECT — then tell me what MATERIAL each one is made from. And could I make this same spoon out of something else?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two-spoons stimulus is identical in object but differs only in material, so it isolates the object/material distinction. A child who has conflated the two answers the 'which is the object' question with a material word ('it's wood') or insists a spoon must be one particular material; a child who holds the distinction separates the thing-and-its-purpose from the stuff and readily agrees the same object could be made from something else.
